title: Lower your voices
hook: don't raise your voices above the Prophet's voice (49:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bay'ah, the promise made hand in hand when the moment wasn't safe. Your line: pledged under the tree.

Two people talking over each other, then three, each a little louder, until nobody is listening and everyone is shouting a point at the ceiling. Usually it's an office or a family dinner. Once, the reports say, it happened in Medina, in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and the two rising voices belonged to Abu Bakr and 'Umar. That scene sits behind Surah Al-Hujurat, the Private Rooms, the forty-ninth surah: short, and something like a manual for how a community talks.

Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Lift not up your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor shout when speaking to him as ye shout one to another." Then a warning: lest your works be rendered vain while you don't notice. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari gives the occasion. A delegation came from the tribe of Banu Tamim, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar disagreed about who should be appointed over them. They argued in front of the Prophet until their voices rose. After this verse, the report says, 'Umar spoke to the Prophet so softly that he sometimes had to be asked to repeat himself. Another Companion took it even harder. Thabit ibn Qays had a naturally loud voice; he was the speaker for the Ansar. When the verse came down he stayed home, convinced his deeds were wasted. The Prophet noticed he was missing, sent someone to ask, and sent back a message: Thabit was not among the people of the fire, but of paradise. The next verse praises those who lower their voices in his presence. Commentators extend the courtesy beyond his lifetime: raising one's voice over his teaching is a related kind of disrespect. You may remember Luqman's advice to his son, earlier this year: walk modestly and lower your voice. Two surahs, two settings, the same instinct. Volume isn't the same as truth. Often it's a sign that listening has stopped.
screen: `LIFT NOT UP YOUR VOICES.` · `ABU BAKR AND 'UMAR, ARGUING.` · `THABIT, LOUD BY NATURE, STAYED HOME.` · `VOLUME ISN'T TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Picture the next room you'll be in with other people: a dinner table, a meeting, a group chat with a voice of its own. Choose one moment there to lower your volume on purpose, especially if you disagree, and let your breath be slow and low now so your body remembers it. If you pray, you can ask for a humble voice.
Abu Bakr. His voice, raised with 'Umar's in front of the Prophet, became the reason this verse came down, and he learned to speak so softly he had to repeat himself. Today's word.
Your line: the humble voice. A lower voice leaves room for listening. That's day five hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to speak quietly in mosques, and visitors to the Prophet's mosque in Medina recall this verse at his grave; scholars also apply it to how hadith and his teaching are discussed.

chat.says: Is the verse about lowering your voice just about good manners?
options: It's about respect: raised voices before the Prophet risked wasting deeds.
It was a rule only for 'Umar, who had a loud voice by nature.

chat.meaning: 49:2 warns that raising voices over the Prophet's could make deeds vain unnoticed; the next verse praises those who lower them.
